questions.prompt: Which relationship fits bark, trunk, leaf and root in the tree example?
options: They are all pieces of luggage
They all mean exactly the same thing
They are parts of a tree
questions.explanation: Thinking of a tree gives each clue a place in the same group.

questions.prompt: Three clues fit your idea but the fourth does not. What should you try?
options: Check another meaning and test the link against every clue
Assume the puzzle has a mistake
questions.explanation: Another meaning may make the awkward clue fit. A useful link explains the whole set.

questions.prompt: What links shift, space and return in the computer example?
questions.explanation: In the stated computer context, all three name keys on a keyboard.

title: How to find the link in a Connections puzzle

sources.name: Merriam-Webster — Bark: a tree covering or a sound

practice: Try a round of Connections and see whether you can find a link that fits the whole set.

sections.html:
Find one relationship that fits every clue. Bark, trunk, leaf and root all fit “parts of a tree”. Yet bark can also be a dog’s sound, as the dictionary shows.

Your first thought is a starting point. Test the whole set before choosing.
sections.title: Start with the first connection you notice

sections.html:
“Things outside” is vague; “parts of a tree” explains this example. Finish the sentence “Each clue is a…” and check that every word fits.

In BrainiLab Connections, choose the relationship from the answer choices. Games with similar names can use different rules.
sections.title: Find a link you can explain

sections.html:
• Same sound: flour and flower are homophones.
  • Opposite jobs: dust a shelf, then dust dough with flour. Explore the two meanings of dust.
  • One category: bark, trunk, leaf and root are tree parts in our example.

These are different kinds of links, not three rules every puzzle must use.
sections.title: Same sound, opposite meanings—or one group?

sections.html:
If three clues fit and one does not, try another meaning for the awkward clue. Give it a different job before blaming the puzzle.

What links shift, space and return in a computer context?

They are keyboard keys. The computer context makes the relationship fit all three.
sections.title: Give the awkward clue another look

sections.html:
After seeing the answer, revisit the clue that held you up. A new meaning is more useful than remembering which button was correct.

sections.title: Make sense of the answer

description: A word can have more than one meaning. Here’s how to spot the connection that fits every clue.
